content: Urinary hesitancy can affect individuals of all ages and both sexes, but it is most frequently observed in older men with an enlarged prostate gland. This condition typically develops gradually over time, and many individuals may not notice it until they experience urinary retention, where they are unable to urinate, leading to bladder swelling and discomfort. Nearly all older men experience some degree of difficulty with dribbling, initiating urination, or having a weaker urine stream. Urinary hesitancy can arise from various causes, including the use of certain medications such as cold remedies, nasal decongestants, tricyclic antidepressants, and anticholinergic drugs used for incontinence. It may also result from an enlarged prostate (benign prostatic hyperplasia), inflammation or infection of the prostate gland (prostatitis), nervous system disorders, recent surgical procedures (postoperative urinary retention), scar tissue in the urethra (stricture), shy bladder syndrome (difficulty urinating in the presence of others), or urinary tract infections. For managing urinary hesitancy at home, it is important to monitor and document your urination patterns and share this information with your doctor. Applying heat to the lower abdomen, specifically the area between the belly button and the pubic bone where the bladder is located, can help relax the muscles and facilitate urination. Staying well-hydrated is essential, and if an infection is suspected, antibiotics prescribed by a doctor will be necessary. Signs of a possible infection include burning or pain during urination, frequent urination, cloudy urine, and a sudden, strong urge to urinate. Additionally, it is important to be mindful of any medications or supplements you are taking. You should contact a medical professional if you experience urinary hesitancy, dribbling, or a weak urine stream and have not yet been evaluated for these symptoms. Seek immediate medical attention if you develop a fever, vomiting, side or back pain, shaking chills, or if you produce very little urine over one to two days. Other concerning symptoms include blood in the urine, cloudy urine, frequent or urgent urination, or discharge from the penis or vagina. Inability to pass urine at all is a medical emergency and requires prompt evaluation. During a medical consultation, your doctor will take a detailed medical history and perform a physical examination, focusing on the pelvis, rectum, abdomen, and lower back. You may be asked questions about the duration and onset of your symptoms, whether they are worse at specific times of the day, and if the force of your urine stream has decreased. They will also ask about any associated symptoms such as fever, pain or burning during urination, cloudy or bloody urine, or back or side pain. A history of bladder or kidney infections, prostate issues, nervous system disorders, recent injuries, surgeries, or procedures involving the pelvis or bladder will also be reviewed. Additionally, your doctor will need to know about all medications you are taking, including over-the-counter drugs. Treatment for urinary hesitancy depends on the underlying cause. Medications such as alpha-blockers are often effective in relieving symptoms. If a bacterial infection is present, antibiotics will be prescribed.
